20515-the-eagle-of-the-empire-a-story-of:
Cyrus Townsend Brady's The Eagle of the Empire, published in 1915, is a novel of Waterloo. Its chapter titles promise a fast campaign tale. Readers meet bearers of evil tidings, marching armies, and the Emperor himself eating and riding toward his fate.

The hero Marteau bargains for a woman, meets Cossacks on the road, and stands a trial of allegiance. A rescue and a siege crowd the middle chapters. Brady, a clergyman turned adventure novelist, wrote the book for the centenary of the battle. It gives Napoleon's last campaign the pace of a boy's adventure story.
20741-the-adventures-of-a-dog-and-a-good:
A dog tells his own tale in The Adventures of a Dog, and a Good Dog Too. The narrator praises the plain speech of dogs over the bent speech of men. Dogs, he says, mean what their tone says, gruff or smooth, sharp or soft.

Through a dog's eyes, human pride and folly look fresh and odd. The book uses animal voice, a trick as old as fable, to mock human ways. Young readers get fun scenes, while older ones catch the satire in this warm animal tale. It is told as a story for the young.

govdocs-archive_org-SmithGeorgeTheJewsAt:
In 1851 the Right Reverend George Smith, Bishop of Victoria, published his account of a mission of inquiry to the Jewish community at Kaifeng, China. He traveled for the London Society for Promoting Christianity Among the Jews, which wanted firsthand word of that distant colony.

Smith describes the synagogue at Kaifeng, its Torah scrolls, and the customs of a community that had lived in China for centuries with little outside contact. His party questioned local Jews and recorded what remained of their Hebrew learning. The narrative is a rare Western eyewitness report on one of the world's most isolated Jewish settlements.
govdocs-archive_org-russian-occultism-vo: Volume 2 of Russian Occultism turns to the fate of occultists under Stalin and to the research of Alexander Barchenko. Barchenko led expeditions and studies that drew Soviet state interest in the 1920s. Under Stalin, occult circles were repressed and their members arrested or shot. The volume gathers that history: secret knowledge pursued in secret, then crushed by a regime that tolerated no rivals.
govdocs-archive_org-the-zend-avesta-2nd-:
The Zend-Avesta is the scripture of Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest living religions. Part II, translated by James Darmesteter for the Sacred Books of the East series, gathers the Sirozahs, Yasts, and Nyayis.

These are hymns and prayers: praises of angels and heroes of the faith, calls to the days of the month, and short litanies for daily use. Darmesteter's translation made the texts readable for English students of religion. As a world classic, Part II shows Zoroastrian worship from inside, in the words its priests preserved for millennia.
one-of-the-28th-a-tale-of-waterloo:
George Alfred Henty wrote this tale of the Waterloo campaign. A. L. Burt published the illustrated edition in New York. Henty also wrote Bonnie Prince Charlie and other boy's histories. Chapter one brings unexpected news to the hero. A country visit and a run-down ship follow.

Later chapters visit a privateer's rendezvous and British cruisers. The hero returns home, then gains a commission. Startling news and a visitor for Mr. Tallboys follow. Service on detachment closes the sample's contents list. Henty mixes real Napoleonic war detail with adventure. Young readers get courage, travel, and battle scenes.
podcast-tuckercarlson-ISETUBf6aoo:
Russell Brand, the comedian turned broadcaster, joins Tucker Carlson for a wide conversation. Its announced subjects include his political fall and his conversations with God. They also include the people he says are trying to imprison him, and a run for mayor. Brand speaks as a man whose fame, legal troubles, and faith now occupy the same stage.

Carlson and Brand share a trajectory: mainstream celebrity, rupture, and reinvention as independent voices claiming persecution by the old order. Their talk moves between prayer and politics without changing gears. The legal matters hanging over Brand are his to describe here, and he describes them as a campaign against him. The episode preserves two of media's most theatrical converts comparing notes on God and grievance for an audience that follows both men closely.
